title: One arrow, two grids: change of basis

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is Jennifer's numbers change and her How chain re-lay along her new arrows, while the arrow itself stays put, when you drag her basis arrow b₁.
interactive.title: Two grids, one arrow
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Your square grid is drawn in faint lines, with i and j. Jennifer's slanted grid sits over it. Her two basis arrows set it: b₁ = (2, 1) and b₂ = (−1, 1), written in your numbers. One arrow runs from the origin to (3, 3). It has two readouts. On your grid it reads (3, 3). On hers it reads (2, 1), because 2 lots of b₁ plus 1 of b₂ is (3, 3). A How button lays her amounts nose to tail along her grid lines. You can drag the tip of b₁ or b₂ to a whole point, and her grid redraws. While her two arrows do not lie on one line, her numbers are worked out again from the new arrows. The How chain re-lays along them. The arrow itself does not move. Under the picture, P is shown with b₁ and b₂ as its columns. P times her numbers gives yours. Here are the screens. 1, show: the arrow, both readouts and the How chain. 2, a puzzle: her numbers are (1, 2). Where does the arrow end on your grid? It offers (0, 3), (1, 2) and (4, 1). 3, show: b₁ is dragged to (1, 1). Her numbers become (3, 0). The arrow stays at (3, 3). The finished picture shows b₁ at (1, 1). 4, a puzzle: what changed for the arrow to (3, 3)? It offers only her numbers for it, the arrow itself, and nothing at all. 5, show: P = [2 −1; 1 1] and the mix of its columns. 2 lots of (2, 1) plus 1 of (−1, 1) gives (3, 3). 6, a puzzle: a grid is made of (1, 2) and (1, −1). Which matrix takes its numbers to yours? It offers [1 1; 2 −1], [1 2; 1 −1] and [2 −1; 1 1]. 7, show: the way back. P⁻¹ = [1 1; −1 2] ÷ 3 takes (3, 3) to (2, 1). One cell of her grid has area 3. That is P's determinant. 8, a puzzle: where does your arrow (1, −1) sit on her grid? It offers (0, −1), (3, 0) and (1, −1). 9, show: a quarter turn, M = [0 −1; 1 0]. A strip of three stages follows her (2, 1). P takes it to your (3, 3). M turns it to (−3, 3). P⁻¹ brings it back to her (0, 3). The labels build up right to left, P⁻¹MP. 10, a puzzle: which product gives the turn in her numbers? It offers P⁻¹MP, PMP⁻¹ and M alone. 11, show: M = [3 1; 0 2] on a new grid of (1, 0) and (−1, 1). In that grid's numbers, b₁ is (1, 0) and goes to (3, 0). b₂ is (0, 1) and goes to (0, 2). Those are the columns of P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]. The move only stretches each of the new arrows. 12, a mixed puzzle: a new grid is (1, 1) and (1, −1), and your arrow is (4, 2). What are its numbers? It offers (3, 1), (6, 2) and (4, 2). 13, a mixed puzzle: a new grid uses (2, 1) and (4, 2). What goes wrong? One offer is that most arrows get no numbers on that grid. Another is that nothing goes wrong. The last is that its numbers are yours halved. Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines.
interactive.ignores: The grids are drawn only inside the view, and only at whole amounts. Both go on for ever. Amounts in between reach every point between the lines. Jennifer's grid keeps your origin. A map grid that also moves the zero point is a shift as well as a change of basis. The pictures stay flat. In space the same rules hold, with three basis arrows and 3 by 3 matrices.

explain.text:
An arrow's numbers are not the arrow. They are the amounts of each basis arrow you lay nose to tail to reach its tip.[^1] Choose a different basis and the same arrow usually gets different numbers. One matrix turns one set of numbers into the other. Its columns are the new basis arrows.

Your grid uses i and j. So the arrow to (3, 3) means 3 lots of i and 3 of j. Now meet Jennifer, who measures with her own two arrows. Her basis is b₁ = (2, 1) and b₂ = (−1, 1), written in your numbers. Two lots of b₁ reach (4, 2). One b₂ on the end reaches (3, 3). So to her, the same arrow is (2, 1). Her numbers mean nothing until you know her arrows. Now move b₁ to (1, 1). The arrow is now 3 lots of the new b₁ and none of b₂. Her numbers read (3, 0). The arrow has not moved. Only b₁ moved, yet both numbers changed. Each number depends on the whole basis.

To turn her numbers into yours, do what the How button does. Take 2 lots of b₁ and add 1 of b₂. You land on (3, 3). A matrix times a column is exactly that sum. It is a mix of the matrix's columns. So put her arrows in as columns. P = [2 −1; 1 1], and P times (2, 1) is (3, 3).[^2] This is the [[change-of-basis matrix]]. Its columns are her arrows written in your numbers. To go the other way, undo P with its inverse. P's determinant is 2 × 1 − (−1) × 1 = 3. That is also the area of one cell of her grid. So P⁻¹ = [1 1; −1 2] ÷ 3. P⁻¹ times (3, 3) is (6, 3) ÷ 3 = (2, 1). Use P by mistake and (3, 3) goes to (3, 6). Multiply back to check. 3 lots of b₁ plus 6 of b₂ lands on (0, 9), not (3, 3). The area is not 0 because b₁ and b₂ are independent. Suppose her arrows lay on one line. Then they would reach only that line. P would have no inverse. Most arrows would have no numbers on her grid at all.

A move can be rewritten for her grid too. A quarter turn anticlockwise is M = [0 −1; 1 0] in your numbers. She wants one matrix that takes her numbers in and gives her numbers out. Start from her (2, 1). P rewrites it as your (3, 3). M turns that to (−3, 3). P⁻¹ brings it back to hers, (0, 3). Check: 3 lots of b₂ is (−3, 3). M is written in your numbers. So her numbers must become yours before M can act. That puts P first. In any product of moves, the first step goes on the right. So the turn, in her numbers, is P⁻¹MP. This [[change of basis]] can make a move far simpler. Take M = [3 1; 0 2] and the grid (1, 0) and (−1, 1). In that grid's numbers, b₁ is (1, 0) and goes to 3b₁, which is (3, 0). b₂ is (0, 1) and goes to 2b₂, which is (0, 2). Those are the columns, so P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]. On that grid the move only stretches each basis arrow. Finding such a grid is how two masses joined by springs come apart into two simple swings. Three-phase work uses a change of basis too. The Clarke transform turns three phase quantities into two parts at right angles.[^3]

**An arrow's numbers are the amounts of each basis arrow. P has the new basis arrows as its columns. It turns new numbers into old, and P⁻¹ turns them back.**

analogy.text: Say a 12 m cable run goes in 3 m lengths of tray. To the fitter it is 4 lengths. On the drawing it is 12 m. One run, two numbers. To turn lengths into metres, multiply by what one length is in metres, 3. To go back, divide by 3. P does the first job, and P⁻¹ the second. P's columns hold what each of Jennifer's arrows is in your units.
analogy.breaks: A tray run has one direction, so each number depends on one unit only. In the plane, each of her numbers depends on both her arrows. Move b₁ alone and both numbers can change. That is how (2, 1) became (3, 0). Her arrows can also slant away from yours. A length of tray cannot.

practice.text:
- Write the new basis arrows in your numbers. Put them in as the columns of P.
- To go from new numbers to yours, multiply by P. That gives the mix of the columns.
- To go from yours to new numbers, multiply by P⁻¹. For a 2 by 2, swap the two diagonal entries. Change the signs of the other two. Divide by the determinant.
- Check by multiplying back with P. You should land on the arrow you started with.
- A move M written in your numbers is P⁻¹MP in the new ones. Read it right to left: into yours, move, back out.

**Rule of thumb:** P goes from the new grid to the old one. If P's determinant is 0, the new arrows are not a basis.

**Worked example:** A grid is made of (3, 1) and (1, 2). What are the numbers for the arrow (5, 5) on it? P = [3 1; 1 2]. Its determinant is 3 × 2 − 1 × 1 = 5. So P⁻¹ = [2 −1; −1 3] ÷ 5. P⁻¹ times (5, 5) is (5, 10) ÷ 5 = (1, 2). Check: 1 lot of (3, 1) plus 2 of (1, 2) is (5, 5).

**Common mistakes**
- Using P where P⁻¹ is needed. P takes the new numbers to yours, not the other way.
- Writing the basis arrows in as rows. They go in as columns.
- Writing PMP⁻¹ for the move in the new grid. The step on the right goes first. It must turn the new numbers into yours.
- Treating the numbers as the arrow. Change the basis and the numbers usually change. The arrow stays where it is.
